prompt: Each firm earns its money in one way. Match each revenue model with the firm that uses it.

pairs.match: An online bookshop buys a novel from the publisher for 11 dollars and sells it on its own site for 18 dollars.
pairs.explanation: The bookshop owns the copy it sells and keeps the gap between what it paid and the shelf price.

pairs.match: A ticket resale site keeps 12 percent of every resold concert ticket and never owns a ticket itself.
pairs.explanation: The site earns a percentage of each completed transaction between independent sellers and buyers.

pairs.match: A razor brand bills 9 dollars a month and ships fresh blades on the first of each month.
pairs.explanation: Revenue arrives as a recurring fee, so the firm's task is to keep members from cancelling.

pairs.match: A pet-supply site charges a dog-food brand each time a shopper clicks its sponsored listing at the top of the results for 'puppy food'.
pairs.explanation: The site sells sponsored placements to a brand inside its own shopping funnel.

prompt: Name the digital business model each firm operates.

cases.text: A mattress maker stops supplying furniture chains and ships its mattresses in boxes straight to buyers who order on its website.
cases.explanation: The manufacturer bypasses the retailers and sells its own brand directly to end consumers online.

cases.text: A medical-supply firm's portal lets hospital purchasing systems reorder gloves automatically at prices set in a yearly contract.
cases.explanation: Both sides are organizations, the catalog is negotiated, and procurement runs system to system.

cases.text: A holiday-rental site lists apartments owned by thousands of hosts and keeps a fee from each booking.
cases.explanation: The site owns none of the apartments. It connects independent hosts with guests and takes a fee per transaction.

cases.text: A pharmacy app charges a sunscreen brand to show its bottle first whenever shoppers search for 'SPF 50'.
cases.explanation: The pharmacy monetizes its shoppers' searches by selling a sponsored placement to a brand.

cases.text: A coffee roaster opens its own online shop so it can learn which blends repeat buyers reorder, instead of selling only through supermarkets.
cases.explanation: Selling direct gives the roaster first-party customer data that the supermarket would otherwise hold.

prompt: Each marketplace faces one of these situations. Name it.

cases.text: A parent finds a maths tutor through a tutoring app, then pays the tutor in cash for every lesson after the first.
cases.explanation: The two sides met on the platform once and moved repeat transactions off it to avoid the fee.

cases.text: A delivery courier keeps three rival delivery apps open on the same phone and accepts whichever order pays most.
cases.explanation: One participant is active on several competing platforms at once, which weakens each platform's pricing power.

cases.text: A new resale app for sneakers launches with no listings, and the few shoppers who visit leave and do not return.
cases.explanation: Buyers will not come without listings, and sellers will not list without buyers.

cases.text: A new used-book marketplace buys 20,000 books itself and sells them for a year before letting outside sellers join.
cases.explanation: The platform seeds the supply side by acting as a first-party retailer before opening to third parties.

cases.text: A new food-ordering app lets the city's five best-known restaurants sell commission-free for their first six months.
cases.explanation: Subsidizing marquee sellers attracts the supply that will draw the first buyers.

prompt: Sort each description into the architecture it describes.

cards.text: Moving the 'add to cart' button means rebuilding and redeploying the whole store application.
cards.explanation: Presentation and commerce engine are one application, so a front-end change touches the back end.

cards.text: A small shop goes live in an afternoon from one all-in-one template.
cards.explanation: Monolithic platforms simplify initial setup for standard web stores.

cards.text: The team builds a new mobile app that reads the same cart and catalog through the existing APIs, leaving the back end untouched.
cards.explanation: The head is decoupled from one back-end commerce engine, and the two talk only through APIs.

cards.text: A web store and an in-store kiosk show different screens but call the same back-end commerce engine.
cards.explanation: Several heads share one decoupled back end.

cards.text: The retailer replaces only its search service with a specialist vendor's, while catalog, cart and payments keep running.
cards.explanation: Composable commerce assembles separate best-of-breed services, so one can be swapped on its own.

cards.text: Content comes from one vendor, payments from a second and search from a third, all orchestrated through APIs.
cards.explanation: Each function is a separate microservice chosen from a specialist vendor.

prompt: A shopper clicks the buy button for a pair of headphones. Put what happens next in order.

steps.text: The commerce engine confirms with the OMS that a pair is in stock and asks the tax engine for the sales tax at the delivery address.
steps.explanation: Step 1: inventory reservation and tax calculation come before any payment.

steps.text: The payment gateway swaps the shopper's card number for a token, so the merchant's servers never hold the number.
A risk model checks the device and how many orders this card placed in the last hour, then the issuing bank is asked to hold the funds.
The order is written to the OMS for the warehouse to pick and pack, and the held funds are captured for settlement.

prompt: Match each funnel stage with the moment in one shopper's purchase of a tent.

pairs.match: Maya taps a link in a hiking creator's video and arrives at an outdoor store's site.
pairs.explanation: A creator partnership brings a prospective shopper to the storefront.

pairs.match: She opens the Tents category, searches '2-person ultralight' and reads two product pages.
pairs.explanation: She navigates the taxonomy, queries internal search and inspects product detail pages.

pairs.match: She adds a tent to her cart, enters her address and card, and submits the order.
pairs.explanation: Cart, checkout, shipping and payment steps end in a confirmed order.

pairs.match: The parcel is dispatched that evening and arrives two days later.
pairs.explanation: Dispatch and last-mile delivery speed belong to fulfillment.

pairs.match: A month later she posts a five-star review and orders gas canisters without clicking an ad.
pairs.explanation: A satisfied buyer reviews and returns without another paid acquisition click.

prompt: Sort each moment into the funnel it belongs to: a person shopping through pages, or an AI agent shopping on a person's behalf.

bins.label: Human shopper on a web page

cards.text: Types 'running shoes' into a search bar and scrolls the results.
cards.explanation: A short keyword query typed into a search bar is the familiar human discovery step.

cards.text: Is told 'waterproof trail shoes, size 43, under 120 euros, delivered by Friday'.
cards.explanation: A multi-constraint goal stated in conversation replaces the short keyword query.

cards.text: Reads the size charts and return policies of six shops at once before anything is shown to the person.
cards.explanation: The agent evaluates several merchants in parallel and compresses the consideration set.

cards.text: Notices the shoe with the large photo at the top of the page first.
cards.explanation: Eye movements and visual prominence shape a human's attention to rank positions.

cards.text: Applies a promotional code and pays with delegated credentials without opening a checkout page.
cards.explanation: Headless APIs and agent payment protocols let an authenticated agent complete checkout without a graphical page.

cards.text: Types a card number and address into the checkout form.
cards.explanation: A graphical checkout form is built for a human typing details.
